newsitem.title: GERMANY: Hijack ends without injury, two surrender.
newsitem.headline: Hijack ends without injury, two surrender.

text.p: A hijack of an Air Malta airliner with about 80 people on board ended peacefully on Monday when two men gave themselves up after handing their weapons to the pilot, German police said.

Police spokesman Werner Schmidt said the two men left the plane with their hands in the air. He said it was not yet clear who the men were or what weapons they had carried but police immediately searched the aircraft and had found no explosives.

Police had earlier reported one hijacker saying he had a bomb and demanding the release of Turkish gunman Mehmet Ali Agca, who is serving a life sentence in Italy after trying to assassinate the Pope in 1981.
The hijack of the Boeing 737 after it left Malta on a flight to Istanbul, Turkey, with 74 passengers and six crew ended without injury.
"The assailants have given themselves up," Schmidt told reporters at Cologne-Bonn airport 15 km (10 km) south of the city of Cologne.

"They gave themselves up after successful negotiations. All the hostages have been released and were unharmed and in good health," Schmidt said. The hijackers had let five people leave the plane earlier, one of them a woman with heart problems.
Schmidt said it was not clear what type of weapons the two were carrying. He said among the hostages there were 17 Turks, 32 Libyans, 32 Maltese, one Russian and one U.S. citizen.

One of the hijackers, who negotiated with police through a Turkish-speaking interpreter, had initially requested an interview with a television crew, but before this could take place the assailants gave themselves up, Schmidt said.
After landing at the busy Cologne-Bonn airport, the airliner stood at a freight section and German police quickly established contact with one of the hijackers.
Police did not say if they yet knew their identities or nationalities but earlier had reported a demand by one of them.
"He asked for Ali Akca, the Pope's (would-be) assassin, to be released," Schmidt said.
Pope John Paul was shot in the hand and abdomen as he rode in an open jeep before thousands at his general audience in St Peter's Square in Rome in 1981. Emergency surgery saved his life.
Agca, whom the Pope later forgave publicly and visited in jail, was wrestled to the ground by pilgrims, including a nun, and is serving a life sentence in Italy.

Air Malta spokesman John Saliba said the plane left Malta for Istanbul at 23.45 GMT and was diverted to Cologne "following a situation that developed on board and demands made by one of the passengers."
The hijacking was the first involving an Air Malta aircraft since the airline was formed in the early 1970s and the first hijack of a flight originating in Malta.
Air Malta has a growing network of services to Europe, North Africa and the Middle East including three weekly flights to Turkey.
